lessons.title: Case Study: Slippage Cost of Executing a Momentum Signal on a Mid-Cap Stock

children.text: This case study applies the spread and market impact tools from this chapter to one specific, common situation: a momentum strategy buying into a breakout. Momentum trades carry every cost already covered, spread and impact, plus one more that is specific to the strategy style itself, and it turns out to be the largest single piece.
The Setup: A Breakout Signal on a Mid-Cap Stock

A momentum strategy's rules trigger a buy when a stock closes at a new 3-month high on above-average volume. A mid-cap stock does exactly that, closing at ₹410, and the strategy decides to build a ₹40 lakh position starting the next morning. The stock has ₹6 crore in average daily traded value and 2.5% daily volatility, typical of an actively traded mid-cap.

children.text: Cost Pieces 1 and 2: Spread and Market Impact

Using the mid-cap spread tier from Lesson 1 and the square-root impact model from Lesson 2, at 6.67% participation and 2.5% daily volatility, the one-way market impact works out to about 0.32%, and the half-spread cost to about 0.06%. Nothing here is new, it is the same two mechanics applied to this specific trade.
Cost Piece 3: The Momentum Tax, Chasing a Price That Is Already Moving

markDefs.definition: The extra cost a strategy pays when the price continues moving in the direction of its own trade during the time it takes to fully execute, common in momentum strategies that enter precisely because a stock is already trending.

children.text: Momentum strategies have a structural problem spread and impact models do not capture: the signal itself is evidence the price is already moving. Completing a ₹40 lakh order at 6.67% of ADV realistically takes a couple of hours, sliced through the morning session to manage impact. During that window, a stock that just broke out to a new high has historically kept drifting in the same direction, before it eventually cools off or reverses. This is sometimes called
, and it is separate from, and additive to, both spread and impact.

body.title: Round-Trip Cost, With and Without the Momentum Drift Component

body.text: Momentum strategies pay for their own signal. The same price move that told the strategy to buy is the move that makes buying expensive, because the market does not pause and wait for you to catch up. In this example, momentum drift alone, ₹12,000, was larger than the entire exit-side cost, and nearly as large as the entry side's spread and impact combined.

children.text: What This Means for Momentum Strategy Design

There is a real tradeoff here, not a fix. Execute faster and market impact rises, since a more urgent order eats deeper into the order book. Execute slower, sliced across a longer window, and impact falls but exposure to further momentum drift grows, since the price has more time to keep running before the order completes. Momentum strategies live with this tension permanently, and a backtest that ignores it by filling the full order instantly at the signal price is not just missing a cost, it is assuming away the central execution problem the strategy actually has to solve.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why does this case study apply the 0.30% momentum drift cost to the entry (buy) side only, and not the exit (sell) side?
options: Exits are always executed by a different, cheaper algorithm
Selling never has a market impact cost, only buying does

The entry chases a fresh breakout signal where the price is actively trending; the exit is a planned trade several weeks later, not a reaction to a signal that is actively moving the price in real time
Momentum drift only applies to mid-cap stocks, not to the exit leg of any trade
body.explanation: Momentum drift cost comes specifically from chasing a price that is moving because of the same signal that triggered your trade. The entry is exactly that situation. The exit, executed on a separate schedule well after the signal, still pays spread and impact, but has no comparable reason to face adverse continuation from a signal it is not chasing.

body.text: A momentum strategy pays spread, market impact, and a third cost neither of the others captures: the price keeps moving in its favor and against its entry price while the order is still being filled, because the signal and the price move are the same thing. In this case study, that third cost alone was larger than the entire exit leg.

points: Momentum strategies face an execution cost beyond spread and impact: momentum drift, the price continuing to move in the trade's direction while the order is still being filled, because the entry signal is itself evidence of an active trend.
In this case study, a ₹40 lakh breakout buy at 6.67% participation cost ₹27,310 to enter and ₹15,310 to exit, a round trip of ₹42,620, roughly 1.07% of order value.
Momentum drift alone accounted for ₹12,000 of that total, more than the entire exit-side cost and nearly as much as the entry side's spread and impact combined.

Faster execution reduces momentum drift exposure but increases market impact, and slower execution does the reverse, a genuine tradeoff momentum strategies must manage rather than a cost that can simply be modeled away.
